quick.happened: US and Israeli strikes on Iran began on 28 February 2026. Eight months on, oil and freight costs are still high, and French diesel hit a record EUR 2.41 a litre in September.
quick.matters: Oil is the link between a Gulf war and your bills. Brent is above $100 a barrel, against $73 before the war, so fuel and food cost more.
quick.next: A run of key dates starts on 20 October. Israel votes on 27 October, the ECB meets on 29 October and the US votes on 3 November.

connect.title: How the Iran war connects to rising fuel prices and the politics of cost-of-living anger, in plain words
paras: The Gulf ships a large share of the world's oil. Most of it must pass through the Strait of Hormuz, a narrow sea gate. When that route is disrupted, fuel costs more for drivers and firms everywhere.
Gulf exports now run at only 60-80% of normal. Brent trades above $100, against $73 before the war. Euro-area inflation rose to 3.8% in September, and French diesel hit a record EUR 2.41 a litre.

The war is eight months old. Pump prices now drive protests in France and Italy, the ECB's rate choice on 29 October, and the US midterms on 3 November. Israel's 27 October vote will help decide how the war goes on.

report.title: What the report says, in plain words
paras: Strikes on Iran began on 28 February 2026 and still disrupt Gulf energy. Gulf exports run at about 60-80% of normal. The key number is EUR 2.41 a litre, the record French diesel price in September.

Winners are oil producers with open routes, such as Venezuela and Alberta. Russia gains only in part. Losers are households in importing countries, central banks, indebted governments, Sudan aid operations and Gulf exporters whose barrels are stuck.

Next come US-India trade talks on 20 October and Israel's vote on 27 October. Then the ECB and Russia's budget reading on 29 October, the Bank of Japan on 30 October, OPEC+ on 1 November and US midterms on 3 November.

quick.happened: On 17 October 2026, unions and housing-rights groups marched peacefully in Portugal for higher wages, better pensions and action on rents and mortgage costs.
quick.matters: Wages lagging rents and living costs is hitting countries that are not in political crisis, so Portugal shows how widespread the squeeze is.
quick.next: No government response or new march date is confirmed. Watch the state budget debate and wage talks, where these demands would become policy.

connect.title: How Portugal's housing and wages marches connect to France's autumn of unrest, in plain words
paras: In both countries, rents and mortgage costs are rising faster than pay. Households feel squeezed. Food, housing and bills take more of each paycheck, and people start to ask their governments for help.

France's unrest began with school blockades over teacher shortages and grew into nationwide cost-of-living protests. About 550,000 people marched on 17 October, and roughly 2,400 were arrested in one day. A presidential election is six months away.

Portugal's march the same day was peaceful, over wages, pensions and housing. Neither event caused the other. Portugal shows the same pressure reaching a country not in political crisis. How France calms or worsens will shape how Europe reads this wave.

report.title: What the report says, in plain words
paras: On 17 October 2026, unions and housing-rights groups marched in Portugal. They want higher wages, better pensions and action on rents and mortgage costs. Sources call the marches peaceful. There is no confirmed turnout figure, so none is given.

Unions and housing-rights groups gain, because their demands are now in the news. Opposition parties may gain too, which is an estimate. The government faces pressure with limited room to spend. Renters, first-time buyers and landlords are also exposed to the squeeze or to tougher rules.

No government response is confirmed, and no new march date is reported. The state budget debate and wage talks are where the demands could become policy. Check current dates. Also watch France, since events there will shape how European governments read this wave.

quick.happened: About 550,000 people marched across France on 17 October, and police arrested roughly 2,400 in one day, after school blockades spread.
quick.matters: France is the eurozone's second-largest economy, so unrest there adds to its borrowing costs and could weaken European support for Ukraine.
quick.next: Moody's reviews France's credit rating on 23 October, and five unions strike on 5 November.

connect.title: How France's unrest connects to the Iran war's fuel shock and Moody's review, in plain words
paras: France buys oil and fuel on world markets. When oil gets dearer, pump prices and freight costs rise, and households feel it.
US-Israel strikes on Iran began on 28 February 2026 and have kept oil costs high for eight months. French diesel hit a record EUR 2.41 a litre in September.

That squeeze turned a school protest into nationwide unrest. Now the unrest makes France look harder to govern. Moody's reviews its Aa3 negative rating on 23 October, with borrowing costs already 1.4 percentage points above Germany's.

report.title: What the report says, in plain words
paras: A school blockade over teacher shortages in Creteil in late September grew into a national cost-of-living crisis. On 17 October about 550,000 people marched, and roughly 2,400 were arrested that day. Looting and arson hit a dozen cities.

Winners: the far-right National Rally, best placed to sell order, and safe havens like German bonds and Swiss francs. Losers: Macron's centrist bloc, Ukraine, shopkeepers (about 1,500 shops damaged), and anyone shipping through France in November.

Moody's reviews France's rating on 23 October. Five unions strike on 5 November. Budget votes follow in a parliament with no majority, and the presidential election rounds are on 18 April and 2 May 2027.

quick.happened: France pays about 1.4 points more than Germany to borrow, the widest gap since the euro-debt crisis.
quick.matters: If France pays more to borrow, it has less for schools and defence, and the stress can pull Italy and Spain along.
quick.next: Moody's reviews France's Aa3 negative rating on 23 October, and the European Central Bank (ECB) meets on 29 October.

connect.title: How French bond stress connects to France's unrest and the ECB, in plain words
paras: France borrows money by selling bonds to investors. Investors treat Germany as the safe choice. When they see more risk in France, they ask for extra interest. That extra is now about 140 basis points (1.4 points) over Germany.

Protests make France look harder to govern. About 550,000 marched on 17 October, and roughly 2,400 people were arrested in one day. Meanwhile euro-area inflation hit 3.8% in September, so the European Central Bank (ECB) may raise rates on 29 October.

This stress sits where both pressures meet. Moody's reviews France's Aa3 rating on 23 October. The ECB says stepping in is not warranted, and higher rates would add to France's EUR 91bn interest bill for 2027.

report.title: What the report says, in plain words
paras: France pays about 140 basis points over Germany to borrow for ten years, the widest since the euro-debt crisis. That is 1.4 points of extra interest. Debt is about 119% of GDP, and France must raise a record EUR 340bn in 2027.

Winners: German bonds and other safe havens, as money leaves French debt, and the National Rally, which gains from market stress. Losers: French taxpayers, French banks and insurers holding French debt, Italy and Spain, and the government.

Moody's reviews France's rating on 23 October. The ECB meets on 29 October and the Bank of Japan on 30 October. Budget votes follow in late 2026, and the presidential election rounds are 18 April and 2 May 2027.

quick.happened: France elects a president on 18 April 2027, with a run-off on 2 May. The National Rally candidate leads at 35-36%.
quick.matters: France is a leading Ukraine backer and pays into the EU budget. The front-runner wants to end Ukraine funding and cut France's EU bill.
quick.next: Moody's reviews France's credit rating on 23 October 2026. The first round follows on 18 April 2027, the run-off on 2 May.

connect.title: How the French election connects to Ukraine aid and the EU budget, in plain words
paras: France has committed about EUR 27bn to Ukraine and co-leads the Coalition of the Willing, a group backing Kyiv. It also pays about EUR 8bn more into the EU budget than it gets back.

Le Pen pledges to end Ukraine funding within six months and cap France's net EU payment at EUR 5bn. Leaders want the 2028-2034 EU budget agreed by end-2026, before the vote. She calls that rush anti-democratic.

The vote on 18 April 2027 decides whether Paris keeps backing Kyiv and a bigger EU budget. The National Rally candidate leads at 35-36%, though Le Pen's eligibility is in legal doubt after a 2025 conviction.

report.title: What the report says, in plain words
paras: France votes on 18 April 2027, with a run-off on 2 May. Macron cannot run again. In October 2026 polls, the National Rally candidate leads the first round with 35-36%.

National Rally wins, as do Moscow and safe assets like German Bunds. Ukraine, Macron's centrist bloc, and backers of a bigger EU budget lose. Importers facing new EU deforestation and carbon-border rules also lose.
Moody's reviews France's rating on 23 October 2026. EU leaders try to agree the budget by end-2026. The first round is 18 April 2027, the run-off 2 May, and the new president takes over in mid-May.

quick.happened: Two days of rioting and looting around Milan's Duomo led to more than 200 arrests on 17-18 October, with clashes in Turin and Bologna.
quick.matters: Prices, wages and housing strain households across Europe, so unrest in one country can quickly become a money-market worry in another.
quick.next: Moody's reviews France's credit rating on 23 October, and the ECB meets on 29 October; both could move Italy's borrowing costs.

connect.title: How Italy's riots connect to France's unrest and the Iran war's fuel prices, in plain words
paras: The Iran war keeps oil expensive, and that shows up at the pump. Italians feel it every time they fill up. Fuel is the most visible price that is rising.

The strikes on Iran began in February 2026 and have kept oil and freight costs high for eight months. France is under the same squeeze: about 550,000 marched there on 17 October, the same weekend as Milan's riots.

The Milan protests cite that price anger. Prime Minister Meloni called a security meeting, but arrests do not change prices, wages or housing. Italy votes in 2027, so order and living costs will both matter.

report.title: What the report says, in plain words
paras: Rioting and looting broke out around Milan's Duomo and lasted a second day. More than 200 people were arrested over 17-18 October. Clashes also hit Turin and Bologna, and the anger centres on the cost of living.

Meloni's camp may gain by looking like the party of order, though polls don't show it yet. Moscow may gain from distracted EU governments. Shops in Milan's centre and squeezed households lose, and so does Italy's borrowing bill if French stress spreads.
Moody's reviews France's rating on 23 October, and the ECB meets on 29 October. France has a national strike on 5 November, so watch whether Italian protesters copy it. Italy votes in 2027.

quick.happened: Italy is due to hold a parliamentary election in 2027, with 30 June listed, though the exact date could shift.
quick.matters: Italy is the euro area's third-largest economy, and its vote helps decide whether Europe's right stays united on backing Ukraine.
quick.next: France votes first, on 18 April and 2 May 2027. Italy's listed election date is 30 June 2027.

connect.title: How Italy's 2027 election connects to France's presidential vote and Ukraine aid, in plain words
paras: Ukraine relies on support from big European countries. Italy's Giorgia Meloni says backing Ukraine is what makes peace possible. France's Marine Le Pen takes the opposite line.
France votes first, on 18 April 2027, with a run-off on 2 May. In October polls, the National Rally candidate leads at 35-36%. Le Pen pledges to end Ukraine funding within six months.
Italy votes next, with 30 June 2027 listed. Its result decides who sets Italy's Ukraine policy. Together, the two votes test whether Europe's right holds one line on Russia or two.

report.title: What the report says, in plain words
paras: Italy is due to vote in 2027, with 30 June listed. In France, the National Rally candidate leads first-round polls at 35-36%. That candidate pledges to end Ukraine funding, the opposite of Meloni's line.

Meloni's Brothers of Italy and Kyiv gain if Italy keeps its Ukraine line and security dominates. Losers could be the centre-left and Five Star opposition, and shops hit by unrest in Milan, Turin and Bologna.
Italy's budget law must pass by year-end, setting the tone on cost of living and security. France votes on 18 April and 2 May 2027. Italy's listed date is 30 June 2027, and it could shift.

quick.happened: Police clashed with protesters in Brussels and Liege on 17 October, after weeks of Belgian high-school protests that copied France's.
quick.matters: Prices have risen faster than many households' pay across Europe, so a French protest wave can spread to other countries, as it did here.
quick.next: Watch whether Belgium calls more protest days and whether France's unrest keeps growing. If France fades, Belgium probably will too.

connect.title: How the Brussels and Liege clashes connect to France's autumn of unrest, in plain words
paras: French high-school students blockaded schools over teacher shortages. Belgian students copied the blockades and the demands a few weeks later.

In France, the blockades grew into nationwide cost-of-living unrest. On 17 October about 550,000 people marched and roughly 2,400 were arrested in one day. The state cannot afford to buy peace, and a presidential election is six months away.

The copied protests then moved from school gates to the streets of Brussels and Liege on 17 October. Belgium's interior minister called it violence, not protest. Whether new French blockades get copied will help decide if Belgium's unrest goes on.

report.title: What the report says, in plain words
paras: On 17 October 2026, police clashed with demonstrators in two Belgian cities, Brussels and Liege. This followed weeks of high-school protests that echoed France's school blockades. We have no reliable figures for Belgian turnout, arrests or injuries.

Possible winners are hard-line parties, which tend to gain when images of disorder spread, and private security firms. Likely losers are shops and cafes near protest squares, commuters facing closures, and Belgian authorities, who must choose between firm policing and concessions.

Watch for new protest days in Belgium, or a shared date from unions or student groups. Watch whether the government acts on protest rules, policing, school funding or prices. Most of all, watch France: if its unrest grows, Belgium's will likely continue.

quick.happened: Spanish demonstrators plan a strike in November over housing and wages, about two weeks before a snap general election. Exact dates are not confirmed.
quick.matters: Pensions are a central issue in the vote, and a new Spanish government could change Spain's stance on the next EU budget.
quick.next: Watch for confirmed strike and election dates, which are not yet set, plus pension pledges from the main parties.

connect.title: How Spain's November strike and snap election connect to France's unrest and the EU budget, in plain words
paras: Rents and wages are squeezing households in France and Spain alike. People in both countries feel prices rising faster than pay. That shared pressure is why anger in one country gets watched in the other.

France's autumn unrest grew from school blockades into cost-of-living protests. About 550,000 marched on 17 October, and roughly 2,400 were arrested in one day. Leaders across Europe are alarmed that it could spread.

Spain's strike comes about two weeks before its snap election. It could shape turnout and the campaign. A new government could change Spain's stance in talks to agree the 2028-2034 EU budget by the end of 2026.

report.title: What the report says, in plain words
paras: Demonstrators in Spain plan a November strike over housing and wages. It is expected about two weeks before a snap general election. Exact dates are not yet confirmed, and pensions have become a central issue.

Parties with a credible pension and housing offer could gain, as could unions and housing campaigners. The government may take the blame when rents and pay lag prices. Renters, younger workers, commuters and firms on strike day may lose out.

Watch for confirmed strike and election dates, and for which groups call the strike. Also watch for pension pledges with costings from the main parties, and any sign French unrest is spreading to Spain.

quick.happened: On 19 October 2026, Putin proposed a summit with Trump and Xi on a Ukraine deal. He again refused to meet Zelensky.
quick.matters: Three big powers could settle a war in Europe without Ukraine or its European backers in the room.
quick.next: Trump and Xi both plan to be at the APEC summit in Shenzhen on 18-19 November, the closest venue.

connect.title: How Putin's summit bid connects to Russia's budget squeeze and the Trump-Xi meeting, in plain words
paras: Russia pays for its war with oil and gas money. Defence now takes a huge share of what the state spends. When that money runs short, Moscow wants the war to end on its terms.
Russia's 2026 deficit is now forecast at 7.345 trillion rubles, nearly double the plan. Oil and gas income fell 17.2% in January-September. Defence is set to take more than a third of 2027 spending.
Putin's call for a summit with Trump and Xi fits that pressure. Trump and Xi are due to meet in Shenzhen on 18-19 November. That meeting decides whether his plan gets a real venue.

report.title: What the report says, in plain words
paras: Putin proposed a summit with Trump and Xi on a Ukraine deal. He said he would not meet Zelensky. That is 3 of the 4 leaders at the table. Rubio also denied any pause in US intelligence sharing with Ukraine.

Winners: Putin, who sets the agenda; Xi, who gains status as a needed party; and Trump, who could play broker. Losers: Zelensky and Ukraine, European backers who would be absent, and the idea of inclusive talks.

Next: Russia's budget gets its first reading on 29 October. US midterms are on 3 November. APEC in Shenzhen runs 18-19 November. EU leaders aim to agree their 2028-2034 budget by end-2026. France votes on 18 April and 2 May 2027.
